explanations.answer: The Jews there were trying to kill Him
explanations.explanation: That's the reason the text gives, baker. John 7:1 says Jesus did not want to travel in Judea "because the Jews there were trying to kill Him." So He stays up in Galilee for now. I think that's one place where staying put is just plain wisdom.

explanations.answer: Roman soldiers were out to arrest Him
explanations.explanation: Good guess, because Rome shows up a lot in the Gospels. But John 7:1 doesn't mention soldiers at all. It says the Jews in Judea were trying to kill Him. So the danger in this verse comes from there, not from a Roman arrest.

explanations.answer: Herod had sent men to capture Him
explanations.explanation: Herod is a name you'll hear in other parts of the Gospels, but he isn't in this verse. John 7:1 says Jesus stayed out of Judea "because the Jews there were trying to kill Him." No Herod, no men sent out. Just that one plain reason.

Right, baker. His brothers say, "Leave here and go to Judea, so that Your disciples there may see the works You are doing." (John 7:3) They name the disciples in Judea as the ones who should see. The text doesn't say why they care about that, so I won't guess.

The chief priests are big names in the Gospels, but they aren't in this verse. His brothers say they want "Your disciples there" to see the works. (John 7:3) That means the disciples in Judea. The priests never come up in what the brothers say.

A king in the crowd would be a big audience, I'll give you that. But the brothers don't mention Herod, or any king. They say, "…so that Your disciples there may see the works You are doing." (John 7:3) Disciples only.

Ooh, this one is a trap, baker. The writer says plainly, "For even His own brothers did not believe in Him." (John 7:5) So the answer is false. They were talking big about showing Himself to the world, and the writer says they didn't believe in Him.
That's right. John 7:5 says, "For even His own brothers did not believe in Him." The word "even" says a lot there. These are His own family, standing right in front of Him, giving Him advice.

That's right, baker. Jesus says, "Although your time is always at hand, My time has not yet come." (John 7:6) Their time is always at hand. His is not yet. I think His brothers could walk out the door any time they pleased, and that's the difference He's pointing to.

That sounds fishy, I know, but Jesus really does say it. John 7:6 reads, "Although your time is always at hand, My time has not yet come." So their time is always at hand. The part that's not yet is His.

explanations.answer: He testifies that its works are evil
explanations.explanation: Yes, that's the reason Jesus gives. He says, "The world cannot hate you, but it hates Me, because I testify that its works are evil." (John 7:7) He tells the truth, and the world hates Him for it. His brothers don't get that treatment, and He says so.

explanations.answer: He takes its crowds away from it
explanations.explanation: Crowds do follow Jesus all over the place, but that isn't the reason in this verse. Jesus says the world hates Him "because I testify that its works are evil." (John 7:7) The reason is what He testifies, not who follows Him.

Caesar, the Roman emperor, never comes up in this passage. Jesus gives His own reason: "…it hates Me, because I testify that its works are evil." (John 7:7) The world He talks about hates Him for what He testifies about its works.

Right, baker. John 7:10 says that after His brothers had gone up, "He also went—not publicly, but in secret." So He told them He wasn't going, stayed behind, and then went up after them, quietly. The text doesn't say more about how He pulled it off, so I'll leave that to the passage.

That would be a parade, and this was the opposite. John 7:10 says Jesus went up "not publicly, but in secret." The text doesn't say He brought the disciples along. Nobody was making a big entrance here.

explanations.answer: Riding in on a young donkey
explanations.explanation: That's a famous scene, but it happens at a different time. (John 12:14) Here in John 7:10, Jesus goes up to the feast "not publicly, but in secret." A donkey ride isn't exactly sneaking. Nobody slips in quietly on a donkey with a crowd cheering.

That's what the text says. Some said, "He is a good man." But others replied, "No, He deceives the people." (John 7:12) Same crowd, same Jesus, two totally different opinions. And they were whispering the whole time.

That charge does come up later in John, but it isn't in this verse. (John 5:16) Here, the others reply, "No, He deceives the people." (John 7:12) Notice they start with "No," because they're answering the ones who called Him a good man.

That sounds close, since Jesus did go up in secret. But the crowd's reply in John 7:12 is, "No, He deceives the people." Nobody in the crowd says anything about Him hiding. They're arguing over whether He's good or deceiving.

I get why you'd think so, since the crowds were buzzing. But John 7:13 says, "Yet no one would speak publicly about Him for fear of the Jews." So the talk was whispering, not open speech. Whispers at a feast, baker. That's a lot of people with something to say and nobody saying it loud.

Right. The crowds were whispering about Him, and John 7:13 says, "Yet no one would speak publicly about Him for fear of the Jews." So the talk stayed quiet. Everybody had an opinion, and nobody wanted to be the one saying it out loud.
